title: NASA’s Artemis II Daily News Conference (April 2, 2026)

segments.text: And here we go.

Good evening, and welcome to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. And welcome to our Artemis two status update. I'm Rachel Kraft with NASA communications, and I'm joined by several NASA managers this evening to talk about our
recent translunar injection burn to send four astronauts on the Artemis two mission to the moon, and about how the test flight is going. Overall, they are Doctor Lori Glaze, who
leads NASA's Artemis program.

Judd Frieling, ascent flight director for the mission, and Howard Hugh Orion, program manager. We'll have some opening remarks and then take questions from reporters here in the room and on the phone.
And those of you who are joining us by phone can press star one to get into the question queue. And with that, we'll start with Lori.
Great. Thank you. Rachel. So ladies and gentlemen, I am so, so excited to be able to tell you that for the first time since 1972, during Apollo 17,
human beings have left earth orbit with Artemis two successful five minute and 52nd Translunar injection burn. This evening, our four crew members NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman,

Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen are now on their trajectory toward the moon. The burn was executed by our flight operations team here in Houston, and it was flawless. The burn
was the last major firing of this mission. From this point forward, the laws of orbital mechanics are going to carry our crew to the moon, around the far side and back to earth.

Our crew is healthy and our spacecraft is performing really well. After we've had a series of checkouts since launch. And again, everything really performing pretty well, and we are on the path that we

designed for this mission. But just a reminder, again, you hear us keep saying it over and over again. This is still a test flight. We are we are getting and we're going to continue to get lots of new data every day. Important
information as we continue learning how we're going to operate this Orion spacecraft in the actual space environment.
And I'll tell you, we're already learning a lot as we go.
We've encountered several things along the way. We're not really tracking anything right now that's of concern, but anything that we've encountered since we've since we've launched was brought to our
mission management team today and discussed and the satisfactory path forward on every case and, and a unanimous decision to proceed forward with the with the go for for
the translunar injection burn.

So you'll hear a little bit more about some of that here in a minute. All the things that we've been doing. So reminder, we got eight days of work ahead and we in turn to learn, learn as much as we can, everything that we can that this vehicle can teach us. And with that. Oh,
let's see, before I do that, I did want to we had a couple images we wanted to share.
Let's see if we can pull some of those up. I wanted to share one of my favorite images. This one I saw last night. Actually, I was, I was getting onto the plane to fly here from Florida.
This one popped up and I just absolutely love this one.

Looking out the window, you can see the solar array wing there and the OMS engine from the Orion spacecraft. And then you can see Earth's crescent in the back. I just thought it was absolutely gorgeous with our crew members being able to see

out the window there and get that, get that photo. It's just absolutely beautiful. And then the second image I wanted to show you, you'll hear a lot more from Howard about the proximity operations demonstration that was conducted yesterday evening.
And let's see, is that one going to come up? Coming back?
It's coming back. There it is.
And in this image you can see Victor Glover on the left.

There he was using the manual controls to maneuver the spacecraft. And then Reid Wiseman on the right there was calling out the commands. So it was really I hope some of you got a chance to watch that. I was riveted. It was absolutely
spectacular to to hear Victor's narration of the whole the whole activity. So super cool.
So with all of that, I am going to hand it over to Judd, and he can talk us through some of the technical details about the flight so far.
All right. Thanks, Lori.

It's been a great couple of days to be in the space business. Yesterday, SLS put us right on the money during ascent. We started with some checkouts by the crew from both the the water dispenser and the
toilet. Those were successful and then burned us with our perigee raise maneuver got us in a stable orbit. We did have a brief comm outage that was due to a ground issue that we
have now rectified, and we understand that's not going to be a problem henceforth. And then let's see, the ISPs then gave us a great amount of
energy, put us in high earth orbit with the apogee raise burn again right down the money.
So really happy with that burn after after that, as Laurie mentioned, Victor did. The ops demonstration gave us a lot of great feedback on on how the the vehicle responds in
preparation for future rendezvous operations. So very valuable data. We also checked out all of the carbon dioxide scrubbers, all three beds successfully checked out, and CO2 is is doing great in the
vehicle. We did once we were done with the the Prox ops demonstration, the ISPs on its own did the automatic deploy of the four CubeSats and then also
ISPs did its disposal burn. And so that all went well. In the middle of the crew sleep. We also had them wake up and do the perigee raise burn, and that was 100% successful. Got
us again, back into a stable orbit, raised our perigee to about 100 nautical miles. So we're happy with that performance as well. This morning the crew woke up. They they had a conference with the
flight control team. And our lead flight director, Jeff Ratigan, went over some details of any anything that they had changes to the timeline, which were minimal. They did an
exercise test of the flywheel that was successful, reported that it was exactly like training. His arms were really, really tired and he got a great cardio workout. So we took some

samples of what the carbon dioxide was while we were doing exercise. And that was all great as well. And of course, just a little under an hour ago, we did the Translunar injection, which sets us up for the free
return around the moon and also for splashdown and San Diego.
So with that, I'll hand it over to Howard to give you some more details on Orion.
All right. Thanks, Jed.
Really excited to be here. Wow, what a great two days. I, I haven't slept, I don't think very much over the last 24 hours, just following all the things that have happened for
the Orion spaceship. We had a perfect ride uphill, got into orbit, spent a good day just checking out systems and getting ready for TLI that Lori
talked about, and a successful TLI and a really good precision burn that we just had. But I'll talk about the things that we accomplished yesterday.

Yesterday, as you know, we did a proximity operations demonstration with the centerline camera and with the spacecraft I call test driving the car. It's been an awesome event for all the engineers and

the team has worked on it. To hear Victor and read, talk about our spaceship and the work that we put in to put into this capability for manual flying. I would say that, first of all, we accomplished all the
test objectives that we set out for this proximity operations.

We have two precision tests, and I'll describe a little bit about what those were, but I'll end with a picture first to show you and describe. This is a very close in picture these three pictures on the upper

left of the picture is our centerline docking target right in the middle. It's a standoff cross that you'll see. It's a two foot wide target. This is the target that we're going to use for future missions. So this is the exact flight

configuration that we use. So it's really important that we got that on the interim cryogenic propulsion stage. So we were able to get that on that stage. And what we do as I describe it, is as we separate
from the ISPs, we do a backflip five degrees per second and we back away all the way. As far in this in this demonstration was about 400ft. And that back

way scenario that allows us to have a good standoff, understanding we're pretty far away. Not this picture, but I'll talk a little bit about where this is going. Then we start doing what I call course manual piloting. And this

allows and you might have heard this, what Victor was doing was basically moving side to side with the spaceship up and down and then doing the rotation pitch roll. Your making sure that the, the response from the

spacecraft and the performance is what he's seeing. And the reason, of course, is because you're so far away at 400ft that you want to make sure you have big maneuvers so you can see the target going out of your field of view a little bit.
Okay, so that's what we did at the initial part. And then we slowly started coming in and approaching the vehicle. And that picture that you see in the upper left side is almost

to 33ft. It's about 40ft away, I think. And that's where we will do what I call fine manual piloting. So we're just doing a little bit of the same thing side to side up and down, doing the pitch roll and yaw maneuver

and handling. And you heard that if you watched closely and some great commentary, especially, it was heartwarming to hear. I know I talked to some of our team members today, you know, to hear that, how
well their baby worked, you know, operating precisely. That is exactly what we wanted to do, holding the attitude and being able to maneuver very well and described, I think, just very

excitedly by read and both Reed and Jeremy, I mean Reed and Victor. I think it's really a great moment for all of us who are have been working in this arena to get this demonstration off. And of course, that wasn't
the end of it. We did back away to about 65ft, and we let the ISPs do a maneuver. And then we had another target, what we were calling the two
dimensional target. So it didn't have a stand off cross like we did on the ISPs. Knows what we did was at a good two degree target or two dimensional target on the on the spacecraft, on the ISPs.
And then we did the same maneuver, but a little different. This maneuver was what we call six degree of freedom maneuver, where we were tracking and also maneuvering by rotating as well. So you're

translating and rotating at the same time. And that allowed you to have a different characteristic of the vehicle performance in a manual piloting approach. And we were also able to go to this 33 foot
range. So really important demonstration of both the fine and coarse handling of the spaceship for future missions as we go forward. And that was something that we wanted to
make sure we brought down some risk. And you saw the images of the centerline camera and performance was outstanding.

And of course the crew was outstanding. They did a terrific job. I actually flew the simulator. I did not qualify for this mission, unfortunately. So definitely wasn't wasn't ready for this kind of mission. But Victor

just did terrific and followed everything. And, and I saw the track today in terms of predictions and I got to give kudos to him. He followed it right along. And it was it was a really great opportunity to

demonstrate our capability. So that was a really important demonstration and test of our rendezvous and prox ops capabilities that we're going to need for the future. But also in that 24 hour period, we
had to obviously demonstrate our readiness for translunar injection. We were able to really track a lot of the subsystems that we've learned from on on Artemis one, but
also the most important subsystem when we put humans on board is the life support system. And I'm happy to report that the performance of the of the CO2 scrubber, the ability
to distribute water, control, the temperature inside the cabin is exactly as we predicted and in some cases better. And so that was really great. And of course, across
all the other subsystems that we demonstrate in this one, like power generation was better than predicted. Also, over 13kW of power generation and our ability to control,

like I said, the inside cabin and control the temperature across all the parts of the spacecraft was right on and nominal. So that was really good to see. And of course, we were ready to execute the TLI
burn today. And our guidance navigation control system was ready to go. And demonstrated through this burn, its its ability to handle this type of burn precision that's needed to
take us to the moon and come back into Earth's atmosphere.
So really great overall demonstration of the Prox ops, really great demonstration of the core subsystems that we have on board the spaceship that's required to execute the rest of the days of this
Artemis two mission. And finally, I would say that we had, I would say, really great opportunity to just understand

our overall performance across all these subsystems and making sure that we're ready to commit the crew to a safe journey to the moon and back. And we demonstrated that over the last 24 hours, we were able to, as
Lori said, have a mission management team review of that and determined that we were go for TLI. And I'm just really happy that we're headed to the moon. Thank you.

All right. It's time now for questions. We'll start here in the room and then we have several on the phone. A reminder, please raise your hand if you're here. We'll have a mic coming around. And then if you are joining by phone
star one can get you into the question queue. And we will begin in the room here. Let's come around with the mic here in the front. Tariq. Yep.
Thank you very much. Tariq Malik with space.com. And I think it's for Howard. You know, the the t l I seem to go quite well, although I guess there were some reports of a couple

of caution alarms that the crew reported. And then the, the mission control said, you know, it was not to worry about. And I'm just curious what those those those alarms were that or those caution lights were. And you know, how they were, I guess set aside so quickly.
Thanks.
I'll let Jed maybe give some highlights there.
Yeah. So about 15, 20 minutes before TLI we had a couple of reconfigure reconfiguration, changes of the atmosphere revitalization system, the cabin fans. And when we were molding those to
different mode, the fan speed change caused the cabin sensors to dip below the caution limit or just a bit. And of course, that rang a alarm that was a suspected cabin leak. It
was a false that was a false indication. And so we quickly knew that there was no leak. We knew that that that it was just the sensors did blow up pretty quickly. Additionally, there were some RCS
reaction control system, SM manifold messages that we had been seeing previously.
Essentially, whenever we're using that system, there's a there's a pressure sensor divergence, and we've seen that before. And so we knew exactly what that those those signatures were. So
again, not an issue at all.
Eric.
Eric Berger.
Ars Technica and just congratulations so far, it's been spectacular to behold all of this. I guess two questions for Howard.
You know, first of all, quik question, were there any thruster issues during the demo, any sort of outages or concerns with that regard? Did everything perform nominally?
And then does the performance and Viktor's piloting during that that exercise give you confidence in Orion's handling for the maneuvers contemplated in Artemis three with 1 or 2 of
the HLS?
Yeah. No issues with the thrusters. They perform nominally, and performance was excellent relative to, you know, future confidence. You know, this gives us a lot of confidence in terms of close in.

I've talked previously about being on the docking axis. It's very important for the crew because unlike orbiter, where we were able to have situational awareness from the windows, when we approach closely, we are very dependent
on the cameras and the lidar that will be on Artemis three and above for our our relative navigation. And so this was a really good exercise of that.
And of course, you know, hearing the crew in a preliminary way through verbally, but we'll look at the data very closely and get the post-flight report from them in detail. I think at first
indication that vehicle performed better than they expected. And I think, you know, for us, it was really a good understanding of how the human loop part worked. We know

precisely what our capabilities are when we have automated capability, but having a crew in the loop and demonstrating their capabilities and being able to hold and be able to execute a translational and rotational maneuvers and be

able to do that precisely, is really outstanding. And I look forward to them coming back home, telling us all the nuances. I'll be sitting in hours with them and questioning them on how they felt about it and what the responses were
based on the pulses they put in.
But yes, it's very, very heartwarming to to hear that from the crew. And of course, even better to get the technical data and play that forward.
Go ahead.
Mark Kirkman with NSF, this is probably for a combination of both Judd and Howard. Now that we're committed with TLI during Translunar coast, the attitude you're going to hold.

What are the out the view windows for the crew? Are they going to be. What are they going to be able to see earth with regard to earth or the moon? And also, prior to the flight you were talking about, based on TLI, what they would get to see when

they do the close observation. It was based on the sun angle of high, medium or low. What did we end up getting based on the launch day and the toy that we're in? And if you don't mind, just based on what he said, I'd like to follow up with Howard.
It sounds like based on what Ike said and you said that the handling qualities, tight deadbeat damping, that this is better than you predicted, is that a true statement?
You want me to start first and talk about that?
I would say that, you know, predictions are hard.

There's a human in the loop kind of element and we practice that. So I would say yes, definitely, maybe better than we anticipated in a lot of ways, because there's variations by which we go into space on a closed loop control system for
guidance, navigation control.

When you have automated system, you know precisely and you predict exactly how the system will respond. The crew is well trained, and Viktor did exactly what he needed to do, and the spacecraft responded.
As far as far as what, where the vehicle will be pointed.
Most of the time we spend in a tail to sun attitude. So we take the back end of the vehicle pointed towards the sun.

And so whatever the geometry is, you know, that's that's what you get. We sometimes have the advantage when we have good power balance, we can move the solar arrays that have cameras on the end, and we can move those around and, and see what,
you know, look back at the earth or look forward at the moon. Also on flight day six, whenever we do, the lunar closer approach will change attitude. Make sure that the crew has those views of the
lunar surface. As far as the lighting of the of the moon, this was a lower, lower lighting day that we launched.
I think it was in the 20 to 30%.
20% lit, you know, area. So we'll still get good, good, you know, shots from the crew will still get great descriptions, you know, from there, you know, Mach one eyeballs. But you know,
I mean it. We're going around the moon. So that's that's the main thing, right? I mean.
Okay, we'll take two more on the end here and then we'll go to the phone. So go ahead.
Jackie.

Hi, Jackie. Wardell, CNN. A quick question for Howard. I know Viktor said that he was going to give the Cooper Harper rating scales during the during the prox ops. Are you able to share those numbers? Just curious to know how it handled.
And then also would love to just ask a general question about the crew, how they're adjusting to orbit.
Specifically curious about the first time flier and whether there's any space adaptation syndrome without, you know, invading privacy. Thanks so much.

Yeah, I'm sure we can share the Cooper Harper handling qualities. I mean, we did assessments with the simulator and we'll do it as part of this demonstration and love to hear that feedback. I think we got
some initial feedback said, but look forward to that. Yeah, definitely. But I'll let you answer the other question about.
As far as the crew members, they're doing great. There's no indication that they're having any problems at all. So I don't expect that they're having any problems.
Hi, Lauren Gresh with Bloomberg. Thanks so much.
And congratulations again.

I wanted to ask about the troubleshooting of the toilet that happened on the first day. Can you just explain to us what the issue was and how they fixed it? And on a priority scale, would you say this was a
number one priority or a number two?
So so, you know, we had always planned to to, to wet the the toilet with some water that we had pulled out of the PWD, the potable water dispenser and, and it turns out,
I guess we didn't put enough in.

And so the, the pump was not fully wetted. And so it has automatic fault detection in that, that if, if it's not, you know, fully wetted, it'll shut itself down. So once we figured out that we didn't put enough
water in, we, we put more in there, made sure that it was essentially primed, the pump was primed, and then the toilet came right back up.

I will say that in addition, a good kind of byproduct of this, while we're working through those procedures, we were able to check out the secondary vent line for the for the urine as well. And so that was a good that's a, that's an

alternate path. If we could not go with the primary line, we were able to bend out on the secondary line. And we were able to demonstrate that. And we did demonstrate today the primary vent line through the working toilet. So I think both
lines are working well and I'm really happy about that.

Yeah. I'll just add real quickly that I think, you know, this is a great example of some of the procedural things as we're learning to work and, and live in the Orion capsule, you know, this is we've got real humans in there. They're trying to live and learn. And, you
know, we're going to we're going to learn things along the way. Oops, we need to do this.
We need to prime it first. This is the kind of things we're we're going to get.
All right. We'll take several questions from the phone now. And we'll start with Marcia Dunn from the Associated Press.
Yes. Hi. Good evening. I have a question probably for you. Lori, could you just sort of or anybody really, could you talk about the stress level in mission control prior to the TLI burn? I mean, were
you really sweating it there? And now that that's done, do you have any new revised numbers for the moon lunar flyby distance?
Do you still think the the Orion is going to go 4000 miles past the moon before turning around, maybe closer to 5000. Any new lunar distance numbers from
today? Thanks.

Hey, Marcia. Thanks for the questions. I'll let Judd speak to what the mood was like down in Mission control. I was actually sitting up, observing the rm and listening in on the loops and, you know, everything was

seemed like it was going very smoothly. They always seem so calm and controlled down there in Mission Control, up in the room where I was with several other folks, you know, as soon as we counted down and we

started that burn, we just sat in silence and watched the clock go and waited for for that statement that said the burn was complete. And that was it was just wonderful to just sit there, watch, enjoy it and
say, you know, we've done this.
So it's a great accomplishment.
We're really proud of all the teams that got us to this point.
Let's see the the second question. Oh, about the distance. So the anticipated distance I believe, was around 4600 miles from the surface. Is that right? And it's it's a good burn. So I'm anticipating
will be pretty close to that, but I don't know that anyone's done the actual calculation yet.
Yeah. Assuming that we had a nominal burn, which we did, the max distance that our folks calculated was 2000 219,639 nautical miles max distance
from the earth.
Yeah.
Okay. So as far as the mood in, in mission control, you know, these teams have done lots and lots of simulations.
And so I would say they're consummate professionals.
Everybody, even with the, the sensor problems that we had able to, you know, do, do the TLI and get us through everything, you know, perfectly.
So, I mean, I wouldn't say there's any stress level at all.

Yeah. Maybe. Lori, I'll jump in on the mission evaluation room that supports the flight control team. You know, I was in there with the team and you know, we have high confidence in our main engine. We've operated several times on Artemis one. And of course we
operated the upper stage separation burn as well. And I'll just tell you everybody was standing not so much nervous, just excitement. And then in one of our conference rooms where we had a couple GNC
experts with us, we geeked out and talked about TGO, Vigo, Lambda, Lambda Dot and teaching a class on how these burns were calculated, what the guidance targets were. And, and it was
really fun to listen to that while we waited for the Tig. So it was really fun.
All right. Our next question on the phone line is from Andrea Leinfelder with the Houston Chronicle.

Hi. I have a question on the exercising. So I was watching the video when Reid was exercising, and I know Mission Control kind of started chuckling because you could see the movement. So I was wondering if you could kind of quantify a little bit

how much it was moving. I know it was expected, but I'm still curious to know how much. Also just a technical question, would you say that Orion was in high earth orbit or low earth orbit during the TLI burn, just because it seems
so close to the earth?
Thanks.

Let me take that. Let's see, as far as the exercise, the I mean, the flywheel machine, it's a little bit like a rowing machine. I think you saw that. I mean, are you asking. I didn't quite understand the
question. Like, how much movement does the capsule do while we're doing the, the, the movement? Is that that the question? Yeah, I didn't I don't think we saw anything that was that we didn't expect.

Yeah. You'll see some solar dynamics which is expected, but it didn't perturb any of our control where we've had to make any adjustments, big burns or anything like that to control the attitude is where you would

hear or get affected by those dynamics. Of course, we'll look at the data. You know, I wasn't sitting in front of the data council today, but well, I just saw it on the videos that were coming down and we'll talk to
the team, but we didn't expect anything different. I asked our guidance navigation guys if there was any issues and they said nope, didn't see any issues relative to exercise.
And then of course, we'll always look at the data and go by that, but looks good so far.
Let's see in the other question was, were we in a high earth orbit when we did TLI?
Yes, technically we were, but we were at the lowest part, you know, perigee of the orbit. So we're about 100 nautical miles off the Earth's surface, traveling about 23 and change
23,000 and change miles per hour. And so because we did the TLI burn, now that takes us out of the high earth orbit and gets us on that free return trajectory to to the side of
the moon.
Okay, next up is Nell Greenfieldboyce with NPR.
Hey, can you hear me?

Okay. Thanks for having this briefing. I would appreciate hearing a little more about the water dispenser situation. It sounded like just before the burn, they were doing what they were calling, like water ops, and they were bagging up water in
plastic bags. Could you just go over exactly what the issues were with the dispenser, and why it was decided to have backup water, and how much water the astronauts actually bagged up? Thank you.
Yeah. Great question. Soe four water tanks in the service module. And each one of those tanks has an isolation valve between them. The the isolation vale
between the middle two tanks failed closed during ascent.
And so it essentially isolated two tanks on one side and two tanks on the other. Each end of those tanks goes to one of two different water dispensers, a
primary and a secondary. So we have full access to all of the water. However, in an abundance of caution, we decided it probably good just in case we have a subsequent failure of of
of an isolation valve to bag some water. And so we, we that's exactly what we did.
We're going to bag some water in the cabin and preserve that just in case we have a subsequent failure.
Okay. Our next question is from Joey Roulette with Reuters.
Hey, thanks. I just wanted to clarify the predicted maximum distance from earth. Did you say 219,000 miles? And is that based on. And that's based on the TLI burn that was
just done today, right?
That those are predicts prior to us performing the burn. So that assumed a perfect TLI burn. So I haven't gone and run those numbers again.
And just real quick, the reason I asked. Of course, is because that's far below the, you know, record breaking for Apollo 13. Is that your guys's understanding? I guess.
That's in nautical miles.
So the Apollo distance recod in nautical miles was about 216,000 nautical miles.
Okay. Our next question is from Jackie Mogensen with Scientific American.
Hi. Thanks for this. I have a bit of a general question and then a specific one. The general one is how do you feel like everything is going to plan?

And are there any concerns you're keeping an eye on at this point? And then more specifically, I was curious if you could tell us about what to expect from the first high res images and video, as well as what we
might see, the solar eclipse. Thank you.

I think I'll take a stab echoing in here. So it's kind of hard to to hear the question, but I think the first one is how things are going. Is there anything we're tracking? And I I'll just look over at my colleagues. But you know,
things are going really well. I think we couldn't be more pleased with how well things are going right now. We're not tracking any issues of concern.

As I said, we're learning from the spacecraft. But that's what we anticipate. And we're not tracking anything. We you know, we went straight into the TLI with absolute confidence that that we can complete this the rest of this mission as planned.

I think the other part of the question had to do with some of the imaging and expectations for when we'll get some of those back. In particular the eclipse. I'm really excited about the eclipse that we're probably going to encounter now

as part of this part of this mission. I think the crew's excited about it as well. I know they did a little training to learn about what they're going to see. It'll be really cool when they're out and beyond the moon. Be able to
look back. With the moon eclipsing the sun, they'll be able to see the sun's corona.
That's kind of a cool, exciting thing to do. So they've been trained on it and they're looking forward to it.
Okay, we'll come back here in the room for other questions.
Let's start here in the second row.

Hi, Michael Atkinson, Houston Public Media. There was a little bit of online chatter about the outlook issues that were happening with Reid Wiseman. I was wondering if you could talka little bit about what exactly was going on with that?
Yeah, this is not uncommon for we have this on station all the time. You know, sometimes outlook has issues getting configured, especially when you don't have a network that's
directly connected. And so essentially we just had to reload his, his, his files on outlook, you know, to get it working.
Okay. Go ahead.
Richard. Two of the post newspaper question for Howard.
You talked earlier about a ground issue related to the communications problem. Can you explain that a little bit more?
Was it literally like a loose screw or was it something underground cabling, maybe a resistance issue? Can you elaborate on that a little bit more? Thank you.
Yeah, I can take that. So so we have a processor at White Sands Ground Terminal. It's called a serial communication processor. In order to get return telemetry it has to
translate the the, the radio messages to something that our front end processors at MCC can, can, can understand. So that processor is supposed to be in a configuration for nominal
S-band Orion telemetry. When we did, we essentially found a bug that we didn't didn't know was there before. So when we did our checkouts, part of our
checkout is to put in a configuration for the emergency comm configuration when we commanded it back to the nominal configuration, it showed that it had taken, but

it did not actually. And so we basically had to go into low level commanding to see what was the actual, you know, configuration and do that. So it's a, it's a software bug we now understand that we hadn't seen before. And so no, no
issue with us, you know, going forward.
Okay, we'll go right here.
Hi, thanks for doing this.

Beverly Casillas for space Scout. So we talked a little bit about some of the communications anomalies and other kind of teething issues we saw in that first day of flight. And I was just curious, what would you say has been the biggest learning moment about
the Orion spacecraft so far during the mission, and have there been any surprises?
Thanks.

Yeah, I think the, the the biggest learning is always first time systems. And I always go to life support, you know, being able to control humidity and scrubbing CO2, which performance is really great. In fact, we're maybe
